notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Ezra 2:24–47, drawn from the approved sources:

---

## Ezra 2:24–35 — The Lay Population (by Towns and Families)

**v. 24 — "the descendants of Azmaveth, 42"**
Azmaveth (called Beth-Azmaveth in Nehemiah 7:28) was a Benjamite town; the name appears in the Benjamin genealogy in 1 Chronicles 8:36. It has been tentatively identified with el-Hizmeh, a height north of Anathoth. The number 42 is the same in both Ezra and Nehemiah, one of the few figures without variation.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-24.htm (Cambridge Bible)
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary

**v. 25 — "the men of Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, 743"**
These three were Gibeonite towns (Joshua 9:17), located near Jerusalem. The grouping of three towns under one number suggests that these small settlements were counted together because individually they had very few returnees. The name in Ezra ("Kiriath-arim") appears with the more correct form "Kiriath-jearim" in Nehemiah 7:29.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-24.htm (Keil & Delitzsch)
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary

**v. 26 — "the men of Ramah and Geba, 621"**
Both were Benjamite towns (Joshua 18:24–25). Ramah is frequently mentioned in the histories of Samuel and Saul. Geba was a Levitical city (Joshua 21:17) and was also spelled "Gaba" (Nehemiah 7:30). The 621 returnees from these two towns are identical in both Ezra and Nehemiah.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-24.htm (Keil & Delitzsch)

**v. 27 — "the men of Michmash, 122"**
Michmash (also spelled Michmas) is known from 1 Samuel 13:2, 5 and Isaiah 10:28. Bob Utley notes the name means "place of Chemosh," indicating a possible ancient pagan association before it became an Israelite town. The number (122) is the same in both Ezra and Nehemiah.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary

**v. 28 — "the men of Bethel and Ai, 223"**
Bethel and Ai were closely associated from the time of Abraham (Genesis 12:8) and Joshua's conquest (Joshua 7–8). Interestingly, Nehemiah 7:32 gives the number as 123 rather than 223 — one of the more notable numerical differences between the two lists, likely a copyist error in one direction or the other.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-24.htm (Keil & Delitzsch parallel table)

**v. 29 — "the descendants of Nebo, 52"**
This Nebo is probably not the Moabite mountain (Numbers 32:3) but a town in Judah. Some suggest it may be Nob (1 Samuel 21:2), or a site called Nuba/Beit-Nuba. Nehemiah 7:33 has "the men of Nebo Acher" ("acher" meaning "other"), which Keil suggests was inadvertently inserted by a scribe anticipating "Elam Acher" ("the other Elam") in the following verses.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-24.htm (Keil & Delitzsch)
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary

**v. 30 — "the descendants of Magbish, 156"**
Magbish does not appear in the Nehemiah list at all, and no town of this name is known. Most scholars regard Magbish as a family name, not a place name. The omission from Nehemiah 7 and uncertainty over the name in 1 Esdras has led some (like Bertheau, cited by Keil) to suggest this entry may be spurious.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-24.htm (Keil & Delitzsch)

**v. 31 — "the descendants of the other Elam, 1,254"**
This is distinguished from the "sons of Elam" in v. 7 (also 1,254). Why two groups bear the same name with the same number is puzzling. Keil and Delitzsch note that "the other Elam" is missing from the 1 Esdras parallel and that the numerical equality with v. 7 is "somewhat strange." They cite Bertheau's view that this entry may be spurious, though they are cautious about dismissing it outright.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-24.htm (Keil & Delitzsch)

**v. 32 — "the descendants of Harim, 320"**
This Harim is a lay family, distinct from the priestly Harim of v. 39 (see note there). Harim means "consecrated." The number 320 is the same in all three parallel lists (Ezra, Nehemiah, 1 Esdras).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-39.htm (Cambridge Bible)

**v. 33 — "the men of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, 725"**
These three towns are in the coastal plain region. Lod (Lydda) and Ono are mentioned in 1 Chronicles 8:12; Hadid is identified with el-Hadithe near Lydda and known from 1 Maccabees 12:38 and 13:13 as Adida. Nehemiah 7:37 gives the number as 721, a minor discrepancy. These towns lay outside the immediate Jerusalem area, showing the returnees resettled a broader territory.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-24.htm (Keil & Delitzsch)

**v. 34 — "the men of Jericho, 345"**
Jericho was the famous city near the Jordan, destroyed by Joshua (Joshua 5:13; 6). The returnees from there numbered 345, identical in all three lists. Men of Jericho are later recorded as helping rebuild the walls under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 3:2).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-24.htm (Keil & Delitzsch)
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary

**v. 35 — "the descendants of Senaah, 3,630"**
Senaah is by far the largest single group in the returning lay population (nearly 3× any other). The location is uncertain: older interpreters identified it with Magdal-Senna, said by Jerome to be seven Roman miles north of Jericho. Nehemiah 7:38 gives the figure as 3,930, a difference of 300. Some commentators have suggested Senaah may represent a larger district or even a collective term including multiple small settlements.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-24.htm (Keil & Delitzsch)
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/ezra/2.htm (noting Michaelis's conjecture that "Senaah" = "the hated one," a title for Jerusalem)

---

## Ezra 2:36–39 — The Priests

**v. 36 — "The priests: The descendants of Jedaiah (through the house of Jeshua), 973"**
The priestly list is identical in names and numbers across Ezra, Nehemiah, and 1 Esdras. Jedaiah was head of the second priestly course under David (1 Chronicles 24:7). The phrase "through the house of Jeshua" is debated: (a) Some (Keil) argue that Jeshua here is the high priest, meaning the Jedaiah family was part of the high-priestly line of Eleazar; (b) the Cambridge Bible suggests Jedaiah is the house (the second of 24 courses) and Jeshua names the particular branch within it — a pattern similar to v. 6 ("Pahath-Moab, of the children of Jeshua and Joab"). Only four of David's 24 priestly divisions returned, and the number of priests (4,289) vastly outnumbered the Levites.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-39.htm (Keil & Delitzsch; Cambridge)
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-39.htm (JFB: "only four of the courses of the priests returned from the Babylonish captivity; but these four courses were afterwards, as the families increased, divided into twenty-four")

**v. 37 — "the descendants of Immer, 1,052"**
Immer was the sixteenth priestly course (1 Chronicles 24:14). Notably, Pashhur the son of Immer was the priest who struck Jeremiah and put him in the stocks (Jeremiah 20:1). The family of Immer was the second-largest priestly group to return.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-39.htm (Cambridge)
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/ezra-2.html (Peake)

**v. 38 — "the descendants of Pashhur, 1,247"**
Pashhur does not appear among the 24 Davidic priestly courses. He is known from 1 Chronicles 9:12 and Nehemiah 11:12 as an ancestor of Adaiah, a priest of the order of Malchijah (the fifth course, 1 Chronicles 24:9). Pashhur son of Malchiah was a prominent figure in Zedekiah's court (Jeremiah 21:1; 38:1). Bertheau (cited by Keil) suggests that Pashhur was a priestly race that grew large enough after David's time to replace an older, perhaps extinct, course. This family became the largest returning priestly group.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-39.htm (Keil & Delitzsch; Cambridge)

**v. 39 — "the descendants of Harim, 1,017"**
Harim was the third priestly course (1 Chronicles 24:8). This is distinct from the lay Harim of v. 32. The name means "consecrated." Members of the priestly house of Harim are later listed among those who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:21).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-39.htm (Benson; Poole; Cambridge)

**Total priests:** 4,289 (973 + 1,052 + 1,247 + 1,017). This is one of the few sections where the numbers are identical across Ezra, Nehemiah, and 1 Esdras.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-39.htm

## Ezra 2:40–42 — Levites, Singers, and Gatekeepers

**v. 40 — "The Levites: the descendants of Jeshua and Kadmiel (through the line of Hodaviah), 74"**
Only two Levitical families returned, and they traced descent to a common ancestor, Hodaviah (also spelled Judah in Ezra 3:9; Hodevah in Nehemiah 7:43). The phrase "through the line of Hodaviah" probably belongs specifically to Kadmiel, to distinguish him from other Levites of the same name. Jeshua and Kadmiel were chiefs of two Levitical orders in Zerubbabel's time (Ezra 3:9) and their names recur in Nehemiah 10:9.

The tiny number — only 74 — is perhaps the most striking figure in the chapter. In David's time there were 38,000 Levites (1 Chronicles 23:3). Several explanations are offered:
- **G. Campbell Morgan:** "Nearly ten times as many priests as Levites went back to the land. This, of course, was an inversion of the original order."
- **David Guzik (Enduring Word):** Some speculate the Levites were particularly invested in worship at the high places, and the purifying fires of exile burned out this idolatrous impulse — so few wanted to return.
- **Bob Utley (Bible.org):** Possibly fewer Levites were exiled in the first place, or temple service seemed too physical and strenuous.
- **Ryrie:** Notes the inferior status of Levites compared to ministering priests.
- **Peake's Commentary:** Observes that by the end of the pre-exilic period all Levites were priests (Ezekiel 48:11ff.), but after the exile a Levite was not necessarily a priest. The tendency to secular life arose during the exile, and Nehemiah 13:10 records Levites abandoning their calling because there was nothing to live on.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-40.htm (Pulpit; Cambridge; Keil & Delitzsch)
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary
— https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezra-2
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/ezra-2.html

**v. 41 — "The singers: the descendants of Asaph, 128"**
The Levitical singers were organised by David into three great guilds: Asaph (a Gershomite), Heman (a Kohathite), and Jeduthun (a Merarite) — see 1 Chronicles 6:33–47; 25:1–7. Remarkably, only the sons of Asaph returned; no descendants of Heman or Jeduthun are listed. Four of the 24 singer classes were from Asaph's line. Asaph himself was a renowned psalmist; Psalms 50 and 73–83 are attributed to him. Nehemiah 7:44 gives the number as 148, a difference of 20.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-41.htm (search excerpt — Cambridge)
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-40.htm (Pulpit; Keil & Delitzsch)
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/

**v. 42 — "The gatekeepers … 139 in all"**
Six families of gatekeepers (or "porters") returned: Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita, and Shobai. Three of these — Shallum, Talmon, and Akkub — had held this office in Jerusalem before the exile (1 Chronicles 9:17). Shallum the chief gatekeeper is also called Meshelemiah (1 Chronicles 9:21), Shelemiah (1 Chronicles 26:14), and Meshullam (Nehemiah 12:25) — illustrating the variety of names or possible textual corruption in these lists. Their duties involved keeping unauthorized persons from forbidden areas of the temple (1 Chronicles 9:26–27). The small number — 139 altogether (138 in Nehemiah 7:45) — reflects the overall scarcity of temple-support personnel among the returnees.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-40.htm (Pulpit; Keil & Delitzsch)
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary (Ryrie; Bob Utley)
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/

**Total Levites (all three classes):** 341 (74 + 128 + 139) — compared to 4,289 priests.

## Ezra 2:43–47 — The Temple Servants (Nethinim)

**vv. 43–47 — "The temple servants: the descendants of Ziha, the descendants of Hasupha, the descendants of Tabbaoth, … Giddel, … Gahar, … Reaiah"**

These are the **Nethinim** (KJV: "Nethinims"), a term meaning "the given ones" (from Hebrew *natan*, "to give"). They were temple servants assigned to assist the Levites with the more menial tasks of temple service. Several important observations from the sources:

- **Origin:** Most commentators trace the Nethinim to the Gibeonites, who deceived Joshua (Joshua 9) and were made "hewers of wood and drawers of water" for the congregation and altar (Joshua 9:27). David Guzik (Enduring Word) cites Trapp: "These were those Gibeonites that, having saved their lives by a lie, were made drawers of water to the temple as a punishment." Bob Utley adds that the unusual non-Jewish names in the list suggest they were descendants of Canaanite slaves, and notes that David also used captured peoples for temple service (cf. 2 Samuel 15:18–22).

- **The term "Nethinim":** The word was originally used for Levites being "given" by God to serve the temple (Numbers 3:9; 8:16), but here it designates a distinct group of non-Israelite descent who performed subordinate duties. Bob Utley also notes that Ezekiel 44:6–31 appears to address this group.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/
— https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezra-2

- **The individual names in vv. 43–47:**
  - **Ziha, Hasupha, Tabbaoth** (v. 43): Ziha and Hasupha appear also in Nehemiah 7:46. Hasupha is also written "Hashupha."
  - **Keros, Siaha, Padon** (v. 44): Siaha is contracted to "Sia" in Nehemiah 7:47.
  - **Lebanah, Hagabah, Akkub** (v. 45): Lebanah appears as "Lebana" in Nehemiah 7:48; Hagabah as "Hagaba." The variations arise from the mutation of Hebrew letters in the Chaldaic dialect. Note: this Akkub among the Nethinim is distinct from the gatekeeper Akkub of v. 42.
  - **Hagab, Shalmai, Hanan** (v. 46): "Shalmai" is a correction (the written text, *Kethiv*, has "Shamlai," which is "evidently a mistake"). Hanan means "[God] is gracious"; it is the root of many biblical names including Hannah, Hananiah, and ultimately "John" (Yohanan = "Yahweh is gracious").
  - **Giddel, Gahar, Reaiah** (v. 47): These names continue into vv. 48–54 in the full list.

The Nethinim as a group totalled 392 persons when combined with the "servants of Solomon" (v. 58), averaging only about nine members per family clan. Some of the names may reflect nicknames or physical characteristics rather than genealogical origins.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The genealogical nature of Ezra 2 means that few directly doctrinal differences emerge among traditions on these specific verses. However, distinct emphases can be noted:

**Reformed/Presbyterian emphasis on covenant continuity:** Steven Cole (Precept Austin, citing Mervin Breneman) stresses that the list demonstrates God's faithfulness to His covenant — He disciplines His people but restores them. The list shows historical continuity between the pre-exilic and post-exilic community. Derek Kidner (Tyndale commentary, cited at Precept Austin) calls the chapter "a monument to God's care."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary

**Baptist emphasis on regenerate church membership:** Matthew Henry (a widely used nonconformist/Puritan voice) draws a spiritual analogy from vv. 36–63: "Those who have no evidence that they are, by the new birth, spiritual priests unto God, through Jesus Christ, have no right to the comforts and privileges of Christians." The exclusion of priests with unprovable genealogy becomes a type of the necessity of belonging to Christ by genuine faith.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-39.htm (Matthew Henry)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik):** Guzik uniquely emphasizes the "purifying fires of exile" as spiritually purging the idolatrous impulse associated with Levitical worship at the high places. He also draws out the personal, human flavour of the names (meanings like "flea," "broad nose," "big belly") — an emphasis on the list as real people, not just data. Guzik notes the absence of Heman and Jeduthun's descendants among the singers, though he does not over-speculate why.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/

**Lutheran:** No distinctively Lutheran reading of these verses was found in the searched sources from lcms.org or 1517.org. The standard Lutheran approach would align with the general conservative Protestant reading while emphasising that God works through means (the ordered temple offices, the careful genealogies) to preserve His people and prepare for the coming Messiah.

**Methodist/Wesleyan:** No Methodist-specific commentary on these verses was found in the searched sources (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com). The traditional Methodist reading would likely follow Matthew Henry or Adam Clarke, focusing on God's providential preservation of the remnant and the spiritual application to the Church.

**Dispensationalist (Ryrie Study Bible, cited at Precept Austin):** Ryrie gives matter-of-fact historical notes — e.g., noting that only 74 Levites returned "probably due to their inferior status in comparison to ministering priests" and that gatekeepers "kept unauthorized people from entering forbidden areas in the Temple." The dispensational emphasis on literal-historical fulfillment of prophecy is implicit throughout.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (text-critical observations):**

Keil & Delitzsch (19th-century German scholarship, still influential) provide the most detailed text-critical analysis. They note that the numerical differences between Ezra and Nehemiah are "owing to mere clerical errors" and that "attempts to reconcile them in various ways cannot be justified." The total of the separate items in Ezra is 29,818; in Nehemiah 31,089; in 1 Esdras 30,143 — yet all three agree on the grand total of 42,360. This unexplained gap of about 12,000 has been variously attributed to women and children, members of northern tribes, or simple omission of some groups in the itemized list.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-24.htm (Keil & Delitzsch)
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary

The Cambridge Bible notes that "it was even conjectured by one commentator (Michaelis) that Senaah was a title (= 'the hated one') given to Jerusalem with reference to its idolatry before the Captivity."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/ezra/2.htm

**Catholic/Orthodox readings:** The search of newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org did not yield specific commentary on these verses. Historically, the Catholic tradition treats Ezra-Nehemiah as canonical history, and the Vulgate's rendering of these names and numbers would align with the received Hebrew text. The Catholic emphasis would be on the institutional continuity of the priesthood — the four returning courses as preserving the legitimate Aaronic priesthood that foreshadows the New Covenant priesthood. The Orthodox tradition reads Ezra as part of the "second canon" (1 Esdras in the Septuagint is used liturgically) and emphasises the restoration of proper worship.

**NET Bible notes (netbible.org):** Not directly accessible in this search round. However, the NET Bible generally provides translation notes on textual variants in these lists, noting where the Hebrew is uncertain.

**Hyper-grace / Prosperity / Word of Faith:** No commentary from these movements on Ezra 2 was found in the searched sources. These traditions typically do not produce detailed verse-by-verse commentaries on genealogical or list passages, focusing instead on promises, blessing, and grace-themed New Testament texts.
